entry.content:
TAROTRON 2000 is a pocket-sized tarot machine I’ve been developing as an experiment in creative technology.

Built using Arduino and an M5StickS3, the prototype runs on a tiny computer with its own screen, speaker and controls. Give it a command and it randomly selects a Rider-Waite-Smith tarot card, displays the card and its meaning, and talks about what it has chosen.

It also has rather more personality than was strictly necessary.

The idea grew out of several strands of my work. I’ve spent more than thirty years working with tarot, built CardMeanings.com as a reference to the 78 Rider-Waite-Smith cards, and I really wanted a new gadget to bring to events. I had been searching on eBay for an 80s electronic tarot toy, only to realise I could make one myself.

The current prototype can select cards, display their meanings, speak, make noises, change its behaviour and occasionally say things it probably shouldn't via a special "Cursed Mode".

I’m now using TAROTRON 2000 to produce a short daily card draw while continuing to experiment with what else this peculiar little machine can do.

If you're curious, follow this silliness at

https://www.youtube.com/@TAROTRON2000
https://www.instagram.com/tarotron2000
https://www.tiktok.com/@tarotron2000

entry.content:
In the latest installment of Tarot DMs, we let a giant Rider-Waite-Smith deck steer a fascinating conversation with award-winning novelist and certified Jungian tarot reader, Jill Dawson, about her newest book, Pixie. Reclaiming the often-misunderstood life of Pamela Colman Smith, the visionary artist behind tarot's most iconic imagery, Jill uses the cards to explore her own creative process. The reading certainly didn't hold back, serving up The Tower to discuss the psychology of catastrophe in her storytelling, the Knight of Wands to reveal how travel sparks her writing synchronicities, and the Seven of Wands to highlight her fierce drive to defend sidelined historical figures with her pen. Packed with brilliant insights from her forty years of working with the cards, and ending with a delightfully nonchalant Page of Cups passed on as a gift for our next guest, this is a chat you won't want to miss.

Head over to the full post on Tarot DMs to read the conversation, and be sure to check out Pixie and jilldawson.co.uk for more of her incredible work.

entry.content:
Step right up and drop your coin in the slot, but be careful what you ask for! In this session, I sat down with director James Crow and screenwriter Simon Cluett to talk about Harbinger, a British horror movie centered around a creepy fairground fortune-telling machine. Built on a deep love for classic scares, the film was a lovenote to old-school Hammer horror. Shot in a real haunted house with deep, moody shadows, it delivered nightmare galore - complete with an appearance by Doctor Who legend Carol Ann Ford!

It felt only fitting to use tarot cards to interview the guys behind a movie where flipping a card had sinister outcomes. With Crow comparing the wild ride of filmmaking to surviving an Evil Dead movie, and Cluett joking that he was typing from inside a protective chalk pentagram, the energy was wonderfully chaotic. Read the full interview below to see exactly what fate dealt them.

entry.content:
How does a 15th-century Italian parlor game become a muse for modern fine art?

In the latest Tarot DMs, Finbarre chats with Claire Gilman (Acquavella Curator at the Morgan Library & Museum) about their packed NYC exhibition, Tarot! Renaissance Symbols, Modern Visions.

We discuss:

  • Pamela Colman Smith’s hidden suffragette nods.
  • Chris Ofili linking the Major Arcana to Trinidadian carnival, and Dorothy Iannone’s delightfully "naughty" custom deck.
  • Drawing the Eight of Swords to explore how tight budgets and space sharpen curatorial vision.

"Artists are drawn to tarot because it has this art-historical lineage... but its symbolism is open-ended enough to speak to contemporary issues."

Read the full conversation on Tarot DMs
